title: How to rewrite a homepage headline
excerpt: Rewrite a homepage headline by naming the audience, the outcome, and the contrast with the old way. The before-and-after lines in this piece are exercises, not client work.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper. Headlines get rewritten by hand, one line at a time.
caption: The line is drafted before it is designed. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a homepage headline?
faqs.answer: Name the audience and the outcome they get. Add the contrast with the old way when that contrast is real. If the line gets long, move the contrast into the sentence underneath. The headline should still be repeatable by a stranger.

faqs.question: Are the sample headlines real client lines?
faqs.answer: No. The before-and-after pairs are invented exercises for the method. They are not projects and not quotes. Run the method on your own offer, then throw the samples away.

faqs.question: Should the on-page headline match the search title?
faqs.answer: They should not contradict each other, and they do not have to be identical. The on-page line is for someone who can already see the product. The title element should tell someone scanning results what the company is, in concise words.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
You can judge homepage headline examples once you treat them as exercises in a method, not as lines to paste onto your site. The method has three parts: name the audience, name the outcome, and name the contrast with the old way. The before-and-after lines below are invented exercises. They are not client work.

The headline on the page and the title in search are related, and they are not the same sentence. Google's guide to [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says the title should be descriptive and concise, and that the main visual title should be obvious. Write the on-page headline for a stranger who can already see your product. Write the title element so someone scanning a results page can tell what the company is.

## The three-part method

Start with the audience, stated as a person with a job. "Clinic managers," "founders hiring their first designer," "shops leaving a patchwork of plugins." If the audience is everyone, the headline will sound like everyone else's. You can widen later. The draft gets sharper when someone specific could hear it and know it is for them.

Add the outcome they get, in language they would use after the work is done. Not the category. The change. "The phone stops being the booking system." "A buyer understands the product without a call." "The catalog and the checkout live in one place." Outcomes are verbs and nouns from their week. They are rarely the word "solutions."

Add the contrast with the old way, if the contrast is real. People understand a new tool faster when they can see what it replaces. The contrast can be a clause, not a second headline. "Invoice software for freelancers who still chase payment in email." The old way is email. The outcome is implied: the chase ends. If you cannot name the old way honestly, skip the contrast. A fake enemy makes the line cute and unclear.

Then cut. The first draft will be long. The headline that remains should still contain the audience and the outcome. The contrast can move into the sentence underneath if the headline gets crowded. A subline is a legitimate part of the method. It is not a place to hide a second, vaguer promise.

## Exercises, clearly labeled

These pairs are practice. Do not publish them as if they were a brand you know.

Exercise A. Before: "Empowering teams to unlock their potential." After: "Hiring software for shops that still track candidates in a spreadsheet." The before names no one and promises a feeling. The after names the audience and the old way. The outcome, a hiring trail that is not a spreadsheet, is visible.

Exercise B. Before: "The operating system for modern commerce." After: "A checkout your warehouse staff can explain to a new hire." The before borrows prestige from a category. The after names an audience, warehouse staff, and an outcome, a process a person can explain. The contrast is the unexplained system they have now.

Exercise C. Before: "Beautiful websites for ambitious brands." After: "A marketing site for founders whose product takes more than one sentence." The before is a taste claim any studio could make. The after names the reader and the problem. It still leaves room for the work to be beautiful. Beauty is no longer doing the job of explanation.

Exercise D. Before: "Next-generation analytics." After: "Weekly numbers for a founder who does not have an analyst." Audience, outcome, and the old way, which is either no numbers or a tool built for a team they do not have. "Next-generation" is the kind of word the method deletes on sight.

Read each after-line and ask whether a stranger could guess the product. If they could, the exercise worked. Then throw the line away and run the method on your own offer. Borrowing an exercise is how homepages start to sound like blog posts about homepages.

## How to test a line without a workshop

Write five versions in a list. Do not design them yet. Read them to someone who does not work on the product and ask them to say back what the company does. Keep the version they can repeat. If they add a word you need, that word belongs in the line. If they shrug, the line is still a mood.

Check the line at phone width. A headline that needs four lines has probably kept a clause that belongs underneath. The first line should still make sense if the rest is cut off by the bottom of the screen. Put the audience or the outcome in that first line, not a windup.

Check it beside the button. The headline and the action should agree. A headline about booking a walkthrough next to a button that says "Start free" is two offers. Pick one. The method's outcome should be the thing the button starts.

Leave the line alone for a day, then delete every adjective and see if the meaning survives. The adjectives that survive are doing work. The ones that do not were decorating a sentence that was afraid to be specific.

## What the headline should not carry

It should not carry the whole brand system, the pricing, and the origin story. Those have places further down, or on other pages. A headline that tries to be a manifesto becomes a paragraph with large type. Large type is not a summary. It is a constraint. Fewer words, more precise nouns.

It should not be a keyword list. Repeating the category in three synonyms does not help a visitor, and Google's title guidance warns that stuffing makes a result look spammy. One clear phrase beats a chain of near-duplicates. If you need a second phrasing for search, put the plain description in the title element and keep the page headline in the company's voice. They should not contradict each other. They do not have to be identical.

It should not depend on a pun the reader has to solve. Cleverness is allowed after the meaning is safe. If the joke is the only version of the offer, the joke has taken the headline's job. Move it to a smaller line, or cut it.

When the product itself is hard to point at, the headline method still applies, and the page around it has more work to do. That case is covered in [what to put above the fold when the product is hard to explain](/blog/homepage-for-a-hard-to-explain-product).

If you want the headline rewritten as part of the page, not as a slogan exercise, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio writes and designs the opening together, so the line and the layout agree.
